summary: Defines naming conventions for describing the different parts of the telephone paths used in Internet emergency preparedness calls, such as those for disaster response. The terms are meant to keep working group discussions and later requirements documents consistent. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When many people talk about an emergency phone system, they need the same words for the same parts. This memo picks the names so everyone is talking about the same thing.

subtitle: Standard names for emergency phone call paths mixing circuit-switched and IP networks.

tldr.problem: The IEPREP (Internet Emergency Preparedness) working group was discussing emergency phone systems but used different terms for the same call architectures, leading to confusion in requirements and design discussions.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines four standard topology names for how emergency calls route through combinations of circuit-switched networks and IP networks: IP Bridging, IP at the Start, IP at the End, and End-to-End IP.
tldr.outcome: Standard terminology lets working groups discuss requirements and solutions with clarity, ensuring everyone refers to the same architecture without misunderstanding.

facts.label: GW definition
facts.value: Gateway (translates CSN to IP or IP to CSN)

today: RFC 3523 is an Informational memo that establishes standard terminology for IEPREP discussions. It does not define protocols or requirements, but rather provides a naming scheme. The four topologies have become standard reference points in emergency communications work, allowing requirements and solutions to be scoped clearly. Later IEPREP and emergency communications documents refer to these topology names when discussing which scenarios they address.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The IEPREP (Internet Emergency Preparedness) working group focuses on enabling emergency communications—calls made during natural disasters, accidents, and other crises where normal network infrastructure may be overloaded or damaged. The group discusses architectures that blend traditional circuit-switched telephone networks with modern IP-based telephony.

However, working group discussions and documents referred to different topologies without consistent naming. Some mentioned "IP in the middle," others discussed "IP on one end," creating confusion about whether documents were addressing the same scenario or different ones. This memo provides a common naming convention so authors and participants can reference the same topologies, focusing discussions and ensuring requirements documents and solutions address the intended architectures.

The memo is deliberately agnostic about the specific signaling protocols (SIP, MEGACO, etc.) or quality-of-service mechanisms (Diffserv, RSVP, NSIS, etc.) used within each topology, so the naming applies regardless of implementation choices.
sections.eli5: Emergency responders talk about phone systems during disasters. Without shared names for different designs, people kept misunderstanding each other. This memo gives the designs names so everyone can talk about the same thing.

sections.title: Four Standard Topologies
sections.content:
The RFC defines four topology types, each combining circuit-switched networks (CSNs) and IP segments with gateways (GWs) that translate between them.

Topology "IP Bridging" (also called "IP in the Middle") has two circuit-switched network endpoints with IP in between. A CSN phone dials another CSN phone; a gateway at one CSN egress point converts the call to IP, the call traverses an IP network, and another gateway at the other CSN's ingress point converts the call back to circuit-switched telephony. This topology is useful when connecting two isolated circuit-switched networks via an IP backbone.

Topology "IP at the Start" has the calling party using an IP phone (computer, PDA, or IP phone hardware), and the called party using a CSN phone. A gateway at the CSN egress point converts the call from IP to circuit-switched when routing to the destination. This topology represents a call from an emergency worker with a mobile device calling someone in the traditional telephone network.

Topology "IP at the End" is the reverse: the caller is on a CSN phone, and the called party is on the IP network. A gateway at the CSN egress ingests the circuit-switched call and converts it to IP for transmission to the IP-based endpoint. Emergency coordinators on the traditional network might use this topology to reach responders with IP phones.

Topology "End-to-End IP" has both the calling and called parties on IP networks with no circuit-switched portions. Both endpoints communicate over IP directly or through IP domains. This is the simplest topology architecturally but may traverse multiple independent IP networks and providers, which can affect call quality and reliability.
sections.eli5: Four common setups: IP bridges two phone networks, IP starts a call and phones finish it, phones start it and IP finishes it, or IP is the whole call end-to-end.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
The RFC introduces two key acronyms for consistency: CSN (Circuit-Switched Network) refers to traditional telephony infrastructure that routes calls on dedicated circuits. GW (Gateway) is a device that converts between circuit-switched and IP protocols, translating call signaling and media streams so endpoints on different networks can communicate.

The document notes that these topologies are media-protocol and signaling-protocol agnostic. An IP segment could use SIP, MEGACO, or another protocol; quality of service could be managed with Diffserv, RSVP, NSIS, or other mechanisms. The topology names refer only to where circuit-switched and IP sections appear in the path, not to the technologies used within those sections.
sections.eli5: CSN is the old phone system; GW is a translator box that lets old phones talk to new IP phones.

sections.title: Impact on IEPREP Work
sections.content:
By establishing these four standard topology names, the RFC provides a foundation for IEPREP working group discussions. Requirements documents can explicitly state which topologies they address. Gap analysis can identify which topologies lack standardized solutions. Solution proposals can be evaluated against all four topologies or focused on specific ones, with clear understanding of scope.

For example, a security solution might address all four topologies equally, or it might be specific to End-to-End IP calls (which have different trust boundaries than topologies that cross CSN/IP boundaries). An interoperability proposal might identify which gateway-to-gateway signaling issues apply to IP Bridging but not IP at the Start. Without these standard names, such distinctions would be buried in lengthy explanations or misunderstood entirely.

The RFC explicitly does not address policy—how to decide which topology to use in a given emergency, or how to prioritize emergency calls within each topology. These policy questions are expected to be addressed in later IEPREP requirements and solution documents, with the topology naming providing the foundation for clear communication.
sections.eli5: Now when the working group writes about emergency phone systems, they can say "we are solving IP Bridging" and everyone knows exactly what they mean.
